name: Aaron Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, that's fine. I don't mind talking. My wife says I talk more about the lathes than about her, so you've picked a good subject.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run three CNC lathes at a company that makes hydraulic fittings, the brass and steel connectors that go on tractors and diggers. CNC just means the machine follows a program, so my job is loading bar stock, setting the tools, checking the first parts with a micrometer and keeping an eye on the wear. Shift starts at seven, finishes at half three, and I'm home before the kids. I like it when a new batch runs clean on the first go. What tires me out is the coolant smell and the evenings when a tool breaks at three o'clock and you know you're staying late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eleven years. Before that I was at a bakery equipment place that closed. So I've been through one shutdown already, which is partly why I'm careful with money now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the stuff that actually matters, like pay and shift patterns. In the break room we already joke that the AI on the office computers mostly writes emails nobody reads. I'd probably share some article about how much money got wasted on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be a bit disappointed. I use one of those chat tools now and then, mostly to explain a drawing note I don't understand or help my son with fractions, and it's handy. But for my job, nothing changing is fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep paying in to the savings, we've got about ten months put by plus the car's paid off. Maybe I'd push the union rep to ask for a pay rise, because if the company's saving time somewhere, we should see some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like after a storm warning that turns into a bit of rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work who'd be pleased with that news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mate Kofi on the next lathe would be smug for a month, he's been saying it's all hype since the start. I'd let him have it. He's usually wrong about football, so he deserves one win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of this that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The robots on our floor aren't AI anyway, they're just arms that load the big machines, and they've been there for years. The machine that worries me isn't the clever one, it's the one that's cheap enough to buy.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about what actually matters, like pay and shift patterns. I'd share some article about how much money got wasted on it.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I use a chat tool now and then and it's handy. But for my job, nothing changing is fine by me.
S0.do: Carries on as he is and keeps paying into savings, which already cover about ten months. Pushes the union rep to ask for a pay rise if the company is saving time.
S0.feel: Calm, like a storm warning that turns into a bit of rain.
S0.quote: The machine that worries me isn't the clever one, it's the one that's cheap enough to buy.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is relaxed and practical, and his past bakery-equipment shutdown explains why he keeps ten months saved. He separates clever AI from cheap machines, and it's the cheap arm he watches. He's fond of his colleague Kofi and tells it with humour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening, so let's get ahead of it as workers, not wait for management to tell us. I'd want the union to ask for training money and a say in which machines come in. Online I'd probably post something about the four-day week, because if robots are doing more, why are we still doing five?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the setting part of my job would shrink. If the machine can set its own tool offsets and check its own parts with a camera, then what's left is loading and unloading, and a robot arm already does that on the big Mazaks. I'd still have work, but maybe less of it, or worse paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few months to see what changes on our floor first. Then, once a couple of the lads had tried it, I'd sign up for the CAM programming course at the college, two evenings a week. That's writing the programs the machines run, and it's the bit I'd want to own. I'd also put another 200 a month into savings instead of the holiday fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a background worry, but I've changed jobs before and come out all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi first, because he won't touch a computer. And Ana in quality, she's fifty-eight and already talking about her pension. I'd try to drag Kofi to the course with me, but he'd say no for a month and then come the week it started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your wife say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya's a nurse, so she's not worried for herself, which helps. She'd say you've complained about that coolant smell for eleven years, maybe this is your way out. And she might be right.

S1.say: It's happening, so let's get ahead of it as workers instead of waiting for management. I'd want training money and a say in which machines come in, and I'd post about the four-day week.
S1.think: I think the setting part of my job would shrink, leaving loading and unloading that a robot arm already does. I'd still have work, but maybe less of it or worse paid.
S1.do: Waits a few months to see what changes on the floor, then signs up for a two-evenings-a-week CAM programming course once colleagues have tried it. Moves an extra 200 a month from the holiday fund into savings.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with background worry, but he's changed jobs before and come out fine.
S1.quote: She'd say you've complained about that coolant smell for eleven years, maybe this is your way out.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron's steady style shows clearly: watch first, then follow the people who tried it. His politics come out as a four-day week and workers' say, not alarm. His wife's job as a nurse gives the household a stable floor, which keeps him measured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs stopping, or at least slowing, until there's a plan. Governments should make the companies pay for it, a robot tax, a basic income, something. I'd sign every petition going and I'd go to the union march, I'd take the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think I'm finished as a machinist. If an AI can program the lathe and a robot can load it, there's nothing I do that it can't. And two years isn't enough for any course to make a difference, because whatever I learned, the AI would learn faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the CAM course idea, no point. I'd keep working as long as they kept me and save every spare bit, and I'd talk to Maya about her picking up extra shifts, since hospitals will need people longest. We'd cancel the summer trip and hold off on Sofia's braces if we could. I'd join anything the union organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, mostly. Angry too, at whoever thought this was a good idea without asking us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what does the time actually allow you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is about how long the shutdown at the bakery place took from the rumours to the last day. I remember how fast that felt, and that was one company. Two years is nothing, it's one apprenticeship that's half finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Daniel, he's ten and he asks everything. I'd tell him Dad's going to be home more and we'll be fine, Mum's at the hospital. I'm not sure I'd believe it while I said it.

S2.say: This needs stopping, or at least slowing, until there's a plan, and the companies should pay through a robot tax or a basic income. I'd sign every petition and take the kids to the union march.
S2.think: I'm finished as a machinist if an AI can program the lathe and a robot can load it. Two years is too short for any course to matter, because the AI would learn faster.
S2.do: Drops the CAM course idea and saves every spare bit while working as long as he's kept on. Asks his wife about extra hospital shifts, cancels the summer trip, delays braces and joins union action.
S2.feel: Scared, and angry at whoever decided this without asking workers.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing, it's one apprenticeship that's half finished.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron's measured style breaks in this scenario: he drops the training he planned in the slower one. He compares two years to the bakery shutdown he lived through, which makes his alarm feel grounded. He leans on his wife's hospital job and on collective action rather than personal plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been warned, so let's use it. Pressure on government to set up retraining and income support now, not in 2030. I'd be pushing that in the union and on the local news Facebook page, where I usually just argue about parking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be forty-eight. I think I'd get maybe three good years at the factory and then it'd thin out. What worries me is that I'd spend those years working for a company that's planning to replace me, and they'd know it and I'd know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see who's actually buying these robots, and then I'd move. Probably into maintenance, because someone has to fix the robots for a while, and I already know the machines. I'd take the maintenance technician course at the college in the evenings, and keep the ten months of savings untouched as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I had a hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move straight away, or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not to start with, no. I'd want to see a few of the robots fail first. I'm not going to be the first one off the boat, but I won't be the last either. That's how I did it at the bakery place too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long do you think maintenance work would last, if robots can do almost anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe three years of steady work, then robots fixing robots. I'm not daft. But three years of a better wage is a lot of mortgage paid.

S3.say: We've been warned, so let's use it and push government for retraining and income support now, not in 2030. I'd push that in the union and on the local news page.
S3.think: I'd get maybe three good years at the factory before it thinned out. I'd be working for a company that's planning to replace me, and we'd both know it.
S3.do: Waits a year to see who's buying the robots, then takes an evening maintenance technician course to move into robot repair. Keeps ten months of savings untouched as a cushion.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a hand on the wheel.
S3.quote: I'm not going to be the first one off the boat, but I won't be the last either.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Aaron's 'wait, then move' habit comes back. He's clear that maintenance work only buys time, but he values those years in mortgage terms. The boat line captures how he places himself among his colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get this right if we start now, so there's no excuse. I'd want the union and the government sitting down together on a proper plan: retraining, shorter weeks, something like a basic income at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I can probably ride this out. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage would be nearly done, and with Maya's job and our savings I could take a few years of lower pay. It's the kids I'd think about more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the maintenance course, but not in a rush, maybe in the second or third year. I'd overpay the mortgage a bit each month, about 150, and start a small savings pot for Sofia's studies. And I'd stay active in the union so we're not caught out at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy. A worry I'd carry around, but not one that stops me sleeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia about her own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia's fourteen and she wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to go for it, but to pick something where people want a person in the room. I'd rather she was the vet the farmer trusts than the one who's cheapest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the end point feel different with ten years, or is it just slower?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, it's the same end. The difference is with ten years I get to pick the moment, and with two years the moment picks me. That's the whole thing, really.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to get this right if we start now, so there's no excuse. I'd want unions and government on a proper plan with retraining, shorter weeks and something like a basic income.
S4.think: I can probably ride this out, since I'd be fifty-three with the mortgage nearly done and Maya's job and our savings behind me. It's the kids I'd think about more than me.
S4.do: Takes the maintenance course in the second or third year without rushing. Overpays the mortgage by about 150 a month, starts a savings pot for his daughter's studies and stays active in the union.
S4.feel: Mostly uneasy, a worry he carries but not one that costs him sleep.
S4.quote: I'd rather she was the vet the farmer trusts than the one who's cheapest.
S4.fieldNote: Aaron sees ten years as letting him pick his moment, which turns alarm into unease. His focus shifts from his own job to his daughter's career choice. He still wants collective planning, consistent with his politics across all five scenarios.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is time, honestly, and if there isn't time, then money while you work out what's next. Something like a year of wages paid by the companies doing the replacing. And proper courses that the college runs with the factories, so you're learning for a real job, not a certificate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask whether people like me get any say in it. Nobody ever asked me if we wanted the robot arm on the Mazaks, it just turned up on a Monday with a ribbon on it. That's how it always goes.

headlineQuote: Nobody ever asked me if we wanted the robot arm on the Mazaks, it just turned up on a Monday with a ribbon on it.
portrait: Aaron Lopez is 43, runs CNC lathes at a hydraulic fittings maker, and is married to a nurse with two children aged fourteen and ten. He lived through a factory shutdown before, so he keeps about ten months saved and watches change before he moves. He stays calm when AI fizzles and plans an evening course when change is steady, but in the two-year AGI picture he drops his plans and leans on his wife's job and union action. With more warning he goes back to waiting, then moving into maintenance, and his thoughts turn to his daughter's future.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years is about as long as his last workplace took to close and no course could make a difference in that time.
whatWouldHelp: Time, or failing that a year of wages paid by the companies doing the replacing, plus college courses run with factories for real jobs.
